paragraphs.heading: Energy without oxygen
paragraphs.text: Fermentation is a kind of anaerobic metabolism that makes adenosine triphosphate (ATP) along with organic end products. A cell breaks down organic molecules such as glucose and other sugars and hands their electrons to other organic molecules. That is the key difference from cellular respiration, where the electrons go to oxygen or to some other inorganic molecule. In 1876 Louis Pasteur called fermentation life without air.

paragraphs.heading: How it works
paragraphs.text: When a cell ferments an organic compound, it splits it into a simpler molecule and frees electrons. Those electrons pass to a carrier called a redox cofactor, such as NAD or ferredoxin, which then hands them on to an organic compound. Glucose first goes through glycolysis or the pentose phosphate pathway and becomes pyruvate. From pyruvate, several routes lead to different end products, such as lactate, and ATP is made along the way.

paragraphs.heading: Cheap but wasteful
paragraphs.text: Fermentation needs no outside electron acceptor, so it can run whatever the surroundings are like. Its main drawback is a low yield: it makes between 2 and 5 ATP molecules per glucose, while aerobic respiration makes 32. It lets organisms gain ATP from organic molecules taken in from outside, such as glucose. The earliest life could not gain energy from it overall, because they were mostly single cells living in an ocean with little complex organic matter.

paragraphs.heading: Who ferments
paragraphs.text: Fermentation happens in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. More than a quarter of bacteria and archaea carry it out, and it is especially common in the phylum Bacillota but rarest in Actinomycetota. Fermenting microbes turn up most often in places tied to a host, such as the gut, but also in sediments and food. Their most common products include lactate, acetate, ethanol, CO₂, succinate, H₂, propionate and butyrate.

paragraphs.heading: Inside our bodies
paragraphs.text: Humans and their livestock gain from gut microbes whose fermentation releases end products the host then uses for energy. Our own bodies ferment too, during exercise and in illnesses such as sepsis and hemorrhagic shock. This supplies energy for somewhere between 10 seconds and 2 minutes, adding to what aerobic metabolism provides. It is held back by the buildup of lactate, and in the end rest becomes necessary.

paragraphs.heading: Food, drink and industry
paragraphs.text: People have used fermentation to make and keep food for 13,000 years, and preserving food is its oldest human use. Fermented foods include cereals, dairy products, rice, honey, bread and beer, and the process is still valued for keeping food and for flavor and texture. On an industrial scale it is perhaps best known for making commodity chemicals such as ethanol and lactate. Ethanol goes into beer, wine and spirits, while lactate can be turned into lactic acid to preserve, cure or flavor food.
